research_thread.scientific_problem: Overcoming the strength-ductility trade-off in tungsten-based alloys caused by brittle precipitates.
research_thread.material_system: Tungsten-based heavy alloys and refractory high-entropy alloys (W-Ni-Fe-Ta).
research_thread.sample_lineage: Traditional single-principal-element alloys (dilute Re, Ti, Cr) vs. Stepwise Controllable Coherent Nanoprecipitations (SCCPs) HEA.
research_thread.intervention: Implementation of a stepwise nano-precipitation strategy (δ-lamellae then γ'' particles) to create coherent interfaces.
research_thread.baseline: Single principal-element alloys and traditional refractory HEAs where secondary phases are intrinsically brittle (silicides, B2, Laves, or brittle W-enriched bcc).
research_thread.conditions: Room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 800°C); thermo-mechanical processing (cold rolling, aging).
research_thread.structure: Dual-phase bcc (W-enriched) and fcc (Ni-Fe-Ta enriched); coherent δ-lamellae and γ'' nano-precipitates with low lattice misfit.
research_thread.outcome: Ultrahigh strength (>2 GPa) combined with sufficient ductility (~15% elongation), defeating the trade-off.
research_thread.mechanism: Coherent interfaces facilitate dislocation shearing and transmission, preventing microcrack initiation at precipitate boundaries, while precipitation hardening provides strength.
research_thread.hypothesis_value: High - Demonstrates a viable pathway to decouple strength and ductility in refractory metals via controlled coherent precipitation.
alternative_explanations: Grain refinement alone could explain strength gains.
Solid solution strengthening is the primary driver rather than coherent precipitation.
boundaries: Strength-ductility trade-off is difficult to solve in single-principal-element systems.
Brittle secondary phases (silicides, B2, Laves) limit ductility in traditional refractory HEAs.
missing_information: Quantitative boundary for lattice misfit tolerance before loss of coherence.
Detailed phase diagram or thermodynamic stability limits of the δ and γ'' phases under varying thermal histories.

evidence_spans: Bulk (W 1.5 Ni 2.25 Fe) 95 Ta 5 (W30-Ni45-Fe20-Ta5, in at.%) alloy ingots were prepared by arc melting pure metals (all with purity >99.99%) in an argon atmosphere.
Alloy samples were repeatedly melted at least 10 times to ensure uniform melting and improve their chemical homogeneity.

After cooling, the bulk ingots with dimensions of 50 mm × 50 mm × 10 mm were homogenized at 1200 °C for 5 h in an Ar atmosphere and subsequently hot-rolled at 1200 °C with a rolling reduction ratio of 80%, i.e., with a thickness reduction from 10 to 2 mm.
After hot rolling, the ingots were rolled at ambient temperature (25 °C) with a reduction ratio of 75% to reduce the thickness from 2 to 0.5 mm (this is termed the cold-rolled alloy).

Following cold rolling, stepwise thermodynamic treatments involving annealing at 900 °C for 5 min (annealed alloy), then aging at 650 °C for 20 h, followed by water quenching, were carried out to obtain the SCCPs structure with δ-lamellas and γ ″ particles.

Dog-bone-shaped specimens for uniaxial tensile testing, with a gauge length of 12.5 mm and a cross-section area of 2.0 × 0.5 mm 2 , were fabricated along the longitudinal direction of the cold-rolled strip material by electro-discharge machining.
The initial as-cast structure of the (W 1.5 Ni 2.25 Fe) 95 Ta 5 alloy has a dual-phase structure with bcc (W enriched) and face-centered cubic fcc (Ni-Fe-Ta enriched) phases

Recrystallization then occurred with the δ-lamella as the source of the nucleation and growth of the fcc grains (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Fig. 3b ); the grain size eventually stabilized at below 1 μm due to a dispersion of the stable δ phase

Indeed, we examined the stability of this phase at elevated temperatures and found that there was no substantial change in size of the γ ″ particles after aging at 800°C for 40 h (Supplementary Figs. 12b and 16b ).

Most importantly, the growth and coarsening of the δ and γ ″ phases, shown in Fig. 2c–f , are both controlled by the sub-micrometer diffusion, which indicates that the formation of both type of precipitates is the result of a diffusional transformation.
